entities.summary:
Hieronymus van Beverningh was a prominent Dutch regent and diplomat who played a crucial role in the Dutch Golden Age. He served as regent for his son, Maurits of Nassau, from 1679 to 1690. During this period, he oversaw significant diplomatic efforts, including the Treaty of Ryswick (1697), which ended the Nine Years' War and established a temporary peace between European powers.

As a patron of the arts, van Beverningh supported prominent artists, such as Johannes Vermeer and Hendrick Willem Mazzotti. He also collected rare books and manuscripts, contributing to the growth of the Netherlands' cultural heritage.

Van Beverningh's legacy extends beyond his diplomatic and artistic pursuits. His influence can be seen in the development of the Dutch East India Company, which became a major player in global trade during the 17th century. As a result, the Dutch Golden Age had a profound impact on European history, shaping the course of politics, culture, and economy for centuries to come.

"legacySummary": "", "summary": "Hieronymus van Beverningh (1614–1690) was a Dutch statesman, diplomat, and regent — one of the most active Dutch diplomatic negotiators of the 17th century, whose career spanned the height of the Dutch Golden Age and the complex European power politics that followed the Peace of Westphalia (1648). A member of the Gouda regent class, Beverningh served as one of the Netherlands' principal diplomats in the critical decades of Anglo-Dutch and European rivalry that shaped the geopolitical order of the late 17th century.

Beverningh's most significant diplomatic roles included participation in the negotiations for the Peace of Westminster (1654) — the peace that ended the First Anglo-Dutch War and that, controversially, contained the 'Act of Seclusion' (secretly negotiated by Johan de Witt, but with Beverningh as a key participant) excluding the House of Orange from stadtholdership; his role in the negotiations for the Treaty of Breda (1667) ending the Second Anglo-Dutch War; and most significantly, his crucial role in the preparation of the 1688 Glorious Revolution — Beverningh was one of the Dutch statesmen who participated in the preparations for William of Orange's invasion of England, helping to secure the constitutional and diplomatic framework that made the Revolution possible.

Beverningh's career illustrates the distinctive character of Dutch Republican foreign policy under the First Stadtholderless Period (1650–1672) and the personal union with England after 1688: the Holland regent class maintained a complex relationship with the House of Orange, alternately supporting and limiting its power, and conducting foreign policy primarily in the interests of Amsterdam commercial capitalism rather than dynastic ambition.
